input: When the transfer processes are considered together, the Chilton-Colburn analogy sets the heat- and mass-transfer factors equal to one another and equal to half the friction factor, in the form $j_D = f/2$, and within the range of conditions the chapter has set out, this equality can be regarded as reasonably serviceable. The point can be made more concrete by a short check on the chapter's own terms: at $f$ = 0.0072 the analogy returns a value of $j_D$ = 0.0036, and a measured factor lying close to that value supports the analogy for the case in hand. The qualification to all of this sits in $f$ itself. Where the measured pressure drop is produced by surface friction alone, $f$ is measuring the same surface process that transfers heat and mass, and the analogy may be expected to hold. Where part of the drop is attributable to form drag — flow normal to a tube bank being the standing example — that part of $f$ has no counterpart in the transfer factors, and $f/2$ will overstate both of them. The analogy therefore fails in a quite definite direction, predicting transfer factors that lie above the measured ones, and it is best confined to the smooth, fully turbulent cases from which it was drawn.
target: For the transfer processes taken together, the Chilton-Colburn analogy sets the heat- and mass-transfer factors equal to each other and to half the friction factor, $j_D = f/2$, and within the conditions the chapter has set out, the equality is serviceable. A short check on the chapter's own terms makes the claim concrete: at $f$ = 0.0072 the analogy returns $j_D$ = 0.0036, and a measured factor close to that value supports the analogy for the case in hand. The qualification sits in $f$ itself. Where the measured pressure drop is produced by surface friction alone, $f$ measures the same surface process that transfers heat and mass, and the analogy holds. Where part of the drop is form drag — flow normal to a tube bank is the standing example — that part of $f$ has no counterpart in the transfer factors, and $f/2$ overstates both of them. The analogy then fails in a definite direction, predicting transfer factors above the measured ones, and it is best confined to the smooth, fully turbulent cases from which it was drawn, and it should not be used outside the range of those cases.
